target: anotoki · genshin_impact API (PHP 8.2 / Slim 4) and Angular frontend
scope: Every HTTP endpoint the API exposes (399 routes), the shared query/model/auth machinery behind them, and the Angular app that calls them. Automated scanning with Semgrep and Psalm, plus a manual read of the parts static analysis is weakest on: authentication, authorization, and anything that turns a request into a filesystem path or a SQL identifier. Revisited on 2026-09-19, after the deploy tooling, the HTTP migrations endpoint, email, the files explorer and the shared set wrappers were added (414 routes): Semgrep and composer audit were run again, and the code added since was read by hand. Psalm was not run again - it is installed on demand into a vendor/ folder that is committed, which is not something to do in passing. SEC-08 onwards come from that revisit. Revisited again on 2026-09-29, after two changes: signing in moved to the anotoki IAM (the registration, password, code, two-factor, session and account endpoints left this site - SEC-01, SEC-04, SEC-09 and SEC-10 were about that code), and the rework that renamed php/ to backend/ and angular/ to frontend/, made every per-installation value required config written by setup.php, and turned setup.php into the development installer too. Semgrep, Psalm (installed into a scratch project and removed after, so the committed vendor/ was never touched) and composer audit were run again, and the new config gate and installer were read and exercised by hand.

tools.name: Semgrep
tools.what: Pattern and dataflow scanner. Backend scanned with p/php, p/security-audit, p/secrets, p/owasp-top-ten; frontend with p/javascript, p/typescript, p/security-audit, p/owasp-top-ten.
tools.backend: 263 files scanned, 0 findings (3 files partially parsed — see note); 2026-09-29, on backend/
tools.frontend: 680 files scanned, 0 findings (2026-09-29, on frontend/src; the one finding of the first run was SEC-07, since fixed)
tools.note: A positive-control file with deliberate SQL injection, command injection and XSS was scanned first and Semgrep flagged all six — so the zero on the backend is a real result, not a broken scan. The 3 parse warnings are files using PHP named arguments (`list: true`) that Semgrep's PHP frontend does not yet accept; those lines were reviewed by hand instead. On the frontend, 2 templates using Angular's @if blocks are parsed partially, for the same reason.

tools.name: Psalm
tools.what: Taint analysis: follows a request value to any dangerous sink (query, filesystem, shell, HTML).
tools.backend: 0 taint findings (2026-09-29; Psalm 5.26.1 on PHP 8.2, types inferred for 71.2%)
tools.note: Psalm inferred types for 71% of this codebase. It is procedural PHP built on global functions and untyped arrays, which is exactly where taint tracking loses the trail — so the zero is corroborating evidence, not proof. The manual review below is what actually clears the dynamic-SQL and path-handling code. It is installed on demand into a scratch composer project and deleted after, never into the committed backend/vendor/.

tools.name: composer audit
tools.what: Checks installed PHP dependencies against the security advisory database.
tools.backend: 0 advisories and nothing abandoned on 2026-09-29 (the first run found 1, slim/slim — SEC-05, since fixed)

findings.title: The JWT signing key is the committed fallback, and this deployment is using it
findings.cwe: CWE-321 Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key
findings.location: php/config/jwt.php:26 — getJwtSecret() (removed 2026-09-28: tokens are the anotoki IAM's)
findings.evidence: No php/config/jwt.local.php exists, so getJwtSecret() returns the string committed in the source: "changeme-create-config-jwt-local-php-with-strong-secret". Confirmed at runtime against the local server — the key in use is the committed fallback.
findings.what: Every session token the API issues is an HS256 JWT signed with this one key. The key is the root of trust for authentication: anyone who knows it can forge a validly-signed token. Because the key is printed in the repository and used as a silent default, it is known to anyone who can read the source, and it is the same on every deployment that never set jwt.local.php.
findings.why: A signature only proves a token came from someone holding the key. If the key is a public constant, the signature proves nothing. The blast radius here is smaller than usual because of two deliberate mitigations, and it is worth being precise about them: (1) the auth middleware looks the token's session up in the database and rejects it unless a live, non-revoked session row exists, so a forged token needs a real session id to name — an attacker with no account cannot mint a working token at all; (2) the user's role is re-read from the database on every request rather than trusted from the token, so a low-privilege user cannot forge themselves an ADMIN token. What remains is still serious: anyone who learns an admin's session id (from a shared machine, a proxy log, a backup, any separate leak) can mint an admin token that the signature check will happily accept, and any account holder can forge tokens for their own session with arbitrary expiry. And the fallback is silent — a production deploy that forgets the file gets a working, insecure system with no warning.
findings.fix: Fail closed instead of falling back. getJwtSecret() should throw if no configured secret is present (no jwt.local.php and no environment variable), so the API refuses to start rather than run on a public key. Generate a real 32+ byte random secret for each environment (`php -r "echo bin2hex(random_bytes(32));"`) and set it via config/jwt.local.php or an environment variable. Add php/config/jwt.local.php to .gitignore — it is not currently listed, so a secret created there could be committed by accident. Rotating the secret invalidates all existing tokens, which signs everyone out once; that is the correct one-time cost.
findings.resolution: Fixed. getJwtSecret() now fails closed — it reads the JWT_SECRET environment variable, then config/jwt.local.php (requiring at least 32 characters), and throws rather than returning a fallback if neither is set, so the API cannot start on a public key. config/jwt.local.php is now in .gitignore, and this environment was given a freshly generated 64-character secret. Rotating the secret signed existing sessions out once, as expected. Since 2026-09-28 the site signs nothing at all: access tokens are issued by the anotoki IAM (../anotoki-iam), whose backend/tests/oidc.test.php holds the tests named here - they are RS256, verified here against its published keys, and its signing key is stored encrypted and rotated under test ('the signing key is stored encrypted', 'rotating the key keeps tokens signed by the old one verifiable'). The one secret left here, config/secret.local.php, is required config with no fallback: without it the API answers 503 not_set_up rather than starting (config/local.php).

findings.title: /api/upload stores an attacker-chosen file extension after only a spoofable type check
findings.cwe: CWE-434 Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
findings.evidence: The type check is `in_array($file->getClientMediaType(), $allowedMimeTypes)` — the Content-Type is supplied by the client and is not verified against the bytes. The stored name is `bin2hex(random_bytes(16)) . '.' . strtolower($ext)` where $ext comes straight from the client filename with no allowlist, and the file lands in public/uploads/, which is Apache's document root in production.
findings.what: An authenticated editor or admin can upload a file whose real content and extension are anything they choose — the MIME allowlist is trivially satisfied by setting the multipart Content-Type header to image/png while the body and extension are something else. The saved file keeps the client's extension and is reachable at /uploads/<folder>/<name>.
findings.why: Two consequences. If the file is a .php, execution is currently blocked only by public/uploads/.htaccess (`php_flag engine off` + RemoveHandler/RemoveType). That works on Apache with mod_php and AllowOverride enabled — but it is the single point of failure, it does nothing under nginx or PHP-FPM, and it fails open silently if the server config changes. Second, even with execution blocked, the router serves uploads with a sniffed Content-Type and no X-Content-Type-Options, so an uploaded .html or .svg is served as a document on the API's origin — stored XSS against anyone who opens the link. The bar is an editor account, so this is a privilege-boundary and account-compromise concern rather than an anonymous one; the sibling endpoint /api/uploads/{entity}/{id}/{field} already does this correctly and is the model to copy.
findings.fix: Validate the extension against a server-side allowlist (avif, png, jpg, webp, gif, opus, mpeg, ogg, wav) and derive the stored extension from a verified type, not from the client filename — reject anything else with 415. Confirm the real content with finfo/getimagesize rather than trusting getClientMediaType(). Serve /uploads with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and, for anything not an image, `Content-Disposition: attachment`. Keep the .htaccess as defense in depth, do not rely on it as the control. Consider retiring /api/upload in favour of the stricter /api/uploads/... path the rest of the app uses.
findings.resolution: Fixed. /api/upload now decides the stored extension from a server-side allowlist (jpg/jpeg/png/webp/avif/gif/mp3/ogg/wav/webm) instead of the client filename, rejecting anything else with 415, and confirms image bytes with getimagesizefromstring so a script renamed to .png does not pass. The client Content-Type is no longer trusted. The dev router and public/uploads/.htaccess now send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and anything that is not an image is served Content-Disposition: attachment, so a stored file cannot render as markup on the API origin. Verified: .php, .html, .svg, an extension-less file, and a fake .png with script bytes are all refused; a real .png is accepted under a randomised name. Correction, 2026-09-19: the Content-Disposition half of that was only ever in the dev router - public/uploads/.htaccess set nosniff alone. See SEC-11, which adds it.

findings.title: No HTTP security headers on API responses
findings.evidence: No response sets Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options / Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors, or Referrer-Policy. The only place these appear is the single hardened /api/files/raw route.
findings.what: The API and the admin panel it backs send no baseline security headers. There is no HSTS to pin HTTPS, no nosniff to stop content-type guessing, no frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options to stop the admin UI being framed, and no Referrer-Policy.
findings.why: None of these is a vulnerability on its own, but together they are the cheap defense-in-depth layer that turns a small mistake elsewhere into a non-event: nosniff neutralises a mislabelled response, frame-ancestors blocks clickjacking of the admin panel, HSTS closes the downgrade window. Their absence is why a header scanner grades this site low, and it is a one-file fix.
findings.fix: Add a small middleware that sets, on every response: `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (or a CSP `frame-ancestors 'none'`), and, once HTTPS is confirmed everywhere, `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`. A JSON API can carry a strict `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` cheaply; the SPA needs its own policy tuned to what it loads.
findings.resolution: Fixed. A middleware now sets X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin and Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none' on every response, and Strict-Transport-Security when the request arrived over HTTPS. It fills in only headers a route did not already set, so the raw-file route keeps its stricter sandbox CSP. Verified against the running server.

findings.title: Registration allows account enumeration and is not rate limited
findings.cwe: CWE-307 Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
findings.location: php/api/routes/users/endpoints/auth.php (POST /api/auth/register) - removed 2026-09-28, registration is the anotoki IAM's
findings.evidence: The handler answers 409 "That email address is already taken" and 409 "That username is already taken", and unlike /api/auth/login it does not call loginAttemptsExceeded() or any throttle.
findings.what: Anyone can probe which email addresses and usernames already have accounts by watching for the 409, and can do so as fast as they like. Each new registration also sends a confirmation email, so the same unthrottled endpoint can be used to send mail to arbitrary addresses.
findings.why: The password-reset endpoint right next to this one is deliberately silent — it gives the same answer whether or not the address exists — which shows the enumeration-resistant pattern was understood. Registration necessarily has to tell a real user their address is taken, so the fix is not silence but a rate limit. Left unthrottled it is both an enumeration oracle and an email-relay for spamming confirmation mails.
findings.fix: Apply the same IP-plus-target throttle the login endpoint already uses (loginAttemptsExceeded / recordLoginAttempt) to registration, and to the confirmation-resend and forgot-password endpoints. Keep the clear 'already taken' message for humans but cap the rate so it cannot be scripted.
findings.resolution: Fixed. Registration now runs the same IP-plus-email throttle the login endpoint uses and records each 'already taken' probe as a non-ok attempt, so a run of enumeration probes trips a 429 while a genuine first signup is untouched. The confirmation-resend and forgot-password endpoints are throttled the same way against mail-spraying, and still answer identically for every address. Verified: repeated register probes and repeated forgot requests for one address both reach 429 after the first handful. Note, 2026-09-19: the two sign-in code endpoints were outside this fix - see SEC-09. Since 2026-09-28 there is no registration here at all: it moved to the anotoki IAM (../anotoki-iam), whose backend/tests/oidc.test.php holds the tests named here, which answers the same for a taken address and throttles by source ('the same answer for a wrong password and an unknown address, and the limiter holds'; 'registration: no session until the link is opened').

findings.title: slim/slim advisory CVE-2026-48157 (reflected XSS in HtmlErrorRenderer) — present but not in the request path
findings.evidence: composer audit reports PKSA-ftt4-t9sz-mwn5 / CVE-2026-48157 against the installed slim/slim. The XSS is in Slim's HtmlErrorRenderer.
findings.what: The installed Slim version carries a known reflected-XSS advisory in the HTML error renderer, which can echo request content into an error page.
findings.why: The app configures the error middleware with displayErrorDetails = false and installs its own JSON default error handler (which the new error-log work confirmed), so the vulnerable HTML renderer is not the one that runs on a failed request. That is a real mitigation, which is why this is Low rather than Medium — but it depends on that configuration staying false, and a dependency with a known advisory should be updated regardless.
findings.fix: Run `composer update slim/slim` to pick up the patched release (>=4.15.2 when available). Keep displayErrorDetails = false in every environment. Re-run `composer audit` in CI so a new advisory surfaces on the next build rather than in the next review.
findings.resolution: Fixed. slim/slim updated 4.15.1 -> 4.15.3; composer audit now reports no advisories. displayErrorDetails stays false, so the HTML error renderer was never in the request path regardless.

findings.title: CORS is handled twice: a correct allowlist that is unused, and a hardcoded localhost origin that is
findings.cwe: CWE-942 Permissive Cross-domain Policy (here: mis-scoped, not over-permissive)
findings.evidence: The live middleware emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:4200` unconditionally. helpers.php contains a correct allowlist (localhost:4200 + https://anotoki.eu) reflecting only matching origins, but nothing calls it in the request path.
findings.what: Two CORS implementations exist. The one that runs hardcodes the development origin; the one that would work in production is dead code.
findings.why: This is not an exploitable hole — the active header is over-restrictive, not over-permissive, and it does not set Allow-Credentials or reflect arbitrary origins, so there is no cross-origin data exposure. But it means the production frontend at anotoki.eu is only reachable if the API is same-origin behind a reverse proxy; if it is ever split onto its own host, CORS breaks, and whoever fixes it in a hurry may reach for a wildcard. The muddle is the risk.
findings.fix: Delete the unused setCorsHeaders()/handlePreflight() in helpers.php, or wire it in and delete the hardcoded block — one CORS path, reading its allowlist from config. Never combine a reflected Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true unless the origin was allowlist-checked first.
findings.resolution: Fixed. There is now one CORS path: a middleware that echoes the request Origin only when it is on the allowlist from corsAllowedOrigins() (localhost:4200 and anotoki.eu, overridable via config/cors.local.php), sets Vary: Origin, and exposes X-Refresh-Token so the token auto-renew works cross-origin. The unused setCorsHeaders()/handlePreflight() helpers were removed. Verified: an allowed Origin is echoed, a stranger Origin gets no CORS header. Since 2026-09-29 the allowlist has no built-in entries at all - the localhost and anotoki.eu defaults are gone: it is this installation's own address and any extra origins from config/app.local.php, written by setup.php. Only while an installation has no config does the API answer any origin, and then only with the fixed 503 not_set_up sentence, which grants nothing.

findings.title: Interpolated href in the site footer
findings.evidence: Semgrep (var-in-href) flagged `<a href="{{ menuItem.url }}">`. The values are site-menu links configured by an admin through the settings area, not free user input.
findings.what: A menu link URL is interpolated into an anchor href. In principle a `javascript:` URL there would run on click.
findings.why: Two things hold it down: the URLs are admin-configured content, not attacker input, and Angular's built-in sanitizer rewrites a `javascript:` URL in an href binding to the inert `unsafe:` form. So this is informational — worth tidying, not a live hole. It is listed because it is the one thing the frontend scan surfaced and it is the right habit to close.
findings.fix: Validate menu URLs to an http/https allowlist when they are saved, and/or bind through a small pipe that rejects non-http(s) schemes, so the intent is explicit rather than resting on the framework's default sanitiser.
findings.resolution: Fixed. The footer now renders a menu link only when isSafeUrl() confirms an http(s) URL, binds it with [href] (so Angular's sanitiser applies) rather than interpolation, and adds rel="noopener noreferrer" to the target="_blank" link.

findings.title: The HTML editor writes stored markup into a live element without sanitising it
findings.evidence: afterValueChange() does `el.innerHTML = value ?? ''` on the contenteditable element, with the value as it came from the database. sanitizeRichHtml is not imported by the component at all - only the preview pane, which renders through app-rich-text, is sanitised. normalizeHtml() likewise assigns the raw string to a detached div's innerHTML, and an `` fires on a detached element too.
findings.what: Rich text that an editor saves is put back into the page as markup the next time anybody opens the same editor. The public site is not affected: everything it renders goes through app-rich-text, whose allowlist held up when it was attacked. The hole is inside the admin panel, between two people who both have accounts - what an EDITOR stores runs in the session of the ADMIN who later opens that record.
findings.why: The two callers both hand the editor database values: the translation HTML modal, and - in the working tree at the time of this revisit - the voice-over text field, which was a plain textarea until it moved to this editor. That move is what widens this from one screen to every character's voice lines. Editors are trusted staff, which is why this is Medium rather than High, but the role split exists so that an editor account cannot act as an admin, and this is a way across it: an `` typed into the editor's source view runs with the admin's token when the admin opens the form.
findings.fix: Sanitise on the way in: `el.innerHTML = sanitizeRichHtml(value ?? '')` in afterValueChange(), the same in the source-view input handler, and have normalizeHtml() parse with DOMParser rather than assigning to a live element's innerHTML. Take care with the comparison that guards the assignment - it compares the element's innerHTML with the incoming value to avoid resetting the caret while typing, so compare against the sanitised string, or typing anything the sanitiser rewrites will reset the caret on every keystroke. That interaction is why this was recorded rather than patched blind: it needs trying in the editor itself.

findings.title: The sign-in code endpoints were not rate limited, and left no trace
findings.cwe: CWE-307 Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
findings.location: php/api/routes/users/endpoints/auth.php - POST /api/auth/login/code and /verify - removed 2026-09-28, sign-in codes are the anotoki IAM's
findings.evidence: Neither handler called loginAttemptsExceeded() or recordLoginAttempt(), while /password/forgot and /confirm/resend beside them call both. SEC-04's fix covered registration, resend and forgot-password; these two were added to the file's family without it.
findings.what: Anyone could ask for sign-in codes for an address, and guess at them, as fast as they liked. issueLoginCode() caps an account at five live codes, but five wrong guesses at /verify burn all five, so asking and guessing in turn sent an address a fresh code for as long as somebody kept going.
findings.why: It is a mail-spraying endpoint and a guessing endpoint with no ceiling, and because nothing was recorded, none of it appeared in the attempts log - the account's owner and the admin user page both showed nothing. Six digits against five guesses per batch is long odds, which is why this is Low; the unbounded mail is the more practical nuisance.
findings.fix: The same two calls, in the same positions, as the endpoints beside them.
findings.resolution: Fixed. Both endpoints now check the limiter before looking the account up - so the 429 says nothing about which addresses exist - and record what happened: `sent` for a request, `bad_code` for a wrong or unknown code. Verified against the running server with a made-up address: the eleventh request for a code, and the eleventh wrong guess, each answer 429. Since 2026-09-28 the endpoints are gone from this site: emailed sign-in codes are the anotoki IAM (../anotoki-iam), whose backend/tests/oidc.test.php holds the tests named here, where every attempt is counted in its login_attempts log and the limiter is under test (the two-factor and sign-in-code cases in 'two-factor: setup, enable, then every sign-in asks').

findings.title: An admin resetting somebody's password left that account's sessions signed in
findings.location: php/api/routes/users/endpoints/users.php - PUT /api/users/{id}/password - removed 2026-09-28, accounts are the anotoki IAM's
findings.evidence: The handler updated the hash and returned a note saying 'Any session they already have stays signed in until its token expires', under a comment that tokens 'are signed, not looked up'. That stopped being true when the auth middleware began validating a session row on every request. Changing your own password (auth.php) already calls revokeSessionsFor() and revokeTrustedDevices(); this path called neither.
findings.what: The reset an admin reaches for when an account is in the wrong hands did not remove the wrong hands. Whoever was signed in stayed signed in for up to the session lifetime, and any device they had marked as trusted went on skipping the second factor.
findings.why: Low because it needs an account to be compromised already and an admin to be responding to it - but that is precisely the moment this endpoint exists for, and it behaved differently from the self-service change in the one way that matters then.
findings.fix: Revoke the account's sessions and trusted devices as the self-service change does, and correct the note.
findings.resolution: Fixed. The reset now ends every session the account has and forgets its trusted devices, with the same two calls the self-service change makes. An admin resetting their own password keeps the session they are doing it from. The note reports how many sessions were ended. Not exercised end to end: it needs an admin sign-in, which this revisit did not have - checked by reading and by php -l, and the calls match the ones already in use. Since 2026-09-28 accounts, and resetting their passwords, are the anotoki IAM (../anotoki-iam), whose backend/tests/oidc.test.php holds the tests named here: a reset ends every session, personal token and outside identity ('a reset takes the account back: sessions, personal tokens and outside identities all go'), an admin-set password forces a change before any application gets a code, and disabling an account ends its sessions everywhere - each under test. This site holds no session to leave behind: it checks the IAM's token on every request.

findings.title: In production, a stored file that is not an image was served inline
findings.evidence: The file's comment said it would 'hand anything that is not an image over as a download', and SEC-02's resolution records that it does. It set X-Content-Type-Options and nothing else; the Content-Disposition rule existed only in router.php, which serves uploads for the development server.
findings.what: The development server was stricter than production. On Apache a stored non-image was served as whatever type it claimed, inline, on the site's own origin.
findings.why: Defence in depth rather than a live hole: the upload allowlist (SEC-02) refuses .html and .svg on the way in, and nosniff stops a mislabelled file being guessed into markup. This is the layer behind those, and it was described as present when it was not - which matters more than the gap itself, because the next person reads the comment and the old report and believes it.
findings.fix: Send Content-Disposition: attachment for everything in uploads/ that is not one of the raster formats an upload may be.
findings.resolution: Fixed. A FilesMatch inside the existing mod_headers guard sends Content-Disposition: attachment for every file that is not avif, png, jpg/jpeg, webp or gif; SVG is left out of that list on purpose. Apache's own syntax check accepts the block, and the pattern was run against sixteen file names, including trick.png.html. Not tried on the production host.

findings.title: Deleted content is still served by the public API
findings.cwe: CWE-212 Improper Removal of Sensitive Information Before Storage or Transfer
findings.location: backend/api/routes/genshin_impact/endpoints/*.php - the list and single GETs; backend/api/full_resource.php
findings.evidence: Confirmed against the running API on 2026-09-19: GET /api/artifacts returned a row with deleted = true (a test artifact), to an anonymous caller. DELETE sets the flag, and the GET handlers fetch without filtering on it. backgrounds.php is the one endpoint file that filters, so the convention exists.
findings.what: Deleting something in the admin panel marks it deleted and nothing else. The public list and detail endpoints go on returning it, and nothing on the public site filters it out again.
findings.why: This is game reference data, not personal data, so the exposure is low - but an editor who deletes a mistaken or unreleased entry reasonably believes it is gone, and it is not. /api/character/random can also hand a deleted character to a quiz.
findings.fix: Filter deleted = FALSE in the list and single GETs and in registerFullResource(), or make DbQuery exclude deleted rows unless asked. It touches some thirty endpoint files and changes what the admin lists show as well, so it wants deciding once rather than patching file by file - which is why it is recorded here and not changed.

findings.title: The admin site guards its tree, but not its admin-only pages
findings.cwe: CWE-602 Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security (here: the absence of the client-side half)
findings.evidence: Since the move to the IAM the admin tree has a canMatch (frontend/src/app/sites/admin/admin-access.guard.ts) that admits only an ADMIN or EDITOR, and the shell draws the no-access page for anybody else. What the first read also asked for is still missing: admin.routes.ts gives its admin-only children (Backups, Settings, Migrations and the other system pages) no role of their own, and the RoleGuard in shared/local-lib/role.guard.ts is still referenced nowhere.
findings.what: An editor is shown pages whose API only answers an admin - the page draws, and every request it makes comes back 403.
findings.why: Not a leak: every endpoint behind those pages enforces its own role, and the review's authorization checks held. It is informational because the server is the control and it holds. What is missing is the client-side half - the panel should not draw itself for someone it is about to turn away.
findings.fix: Per-page roles for the admin-only children, from the same list the API's ROLES_SYSTEM_* groups name. Delete the unused RoleGuard or wire it in; as it stands it navigates to a route that does not exist.

cleared.detail: Every query is parameterised. Table and column identifiers in the DbQuery builder are either hardcoded string literals at the call sites or whitelisted through the DTO reflection layer (fromBody / partialToDbArray only accept declared constructor fields, so an attacker cannot introduce a column). The dynamic WHERE builders (audit logs, users, sessions) bind every value with a placeholder and use only literal column names. INSERT/UPDATE column lists come from whitelisted keys, values are bound. Confirmed by hand across the builder and its callers, and by Semgrep and Psalm.

Every per-user route enforces ownership: path-parameter routes use requireSelfOrAdmin('user_id'), body routes use refuseForeignUserId(), and the quiz convenience endpoints derive the user id from the token rather than accepting one. Checked across quiz-states, quiz-stats-history, user-quiz-history, quiz progress, and the self-service auth routes; the session-revoke route scopes its query to the caller's own user id.

Asset paths are sanitised per segment (separators and control chars stripped, '.'/'..'/dotfiles rejected) and then re-checked with realpath() against the assets root. Backup download/preview constrain the id to a strict timestamp regex and whitelist the database alias; the migrations-file endpoint whitelists the alias and requires basename($f) === $f with a .sql suffix. All admin-gated.

Passwords hashed with password_hash (bcrypt) and checked with password_verify. Reset/confirm/session/device tokens come from random_bytes (CSPRNG) and are stored as SHA-256 hashes, so a database leak exposes no usable token. TOTP codes are compared with hash_equals (timing-safe). JWT verification recomputes HS256 over the header/payload and ignores the token's own alg header, so there is no alg-confusion or 'none' bypass. Sessions are server-side and revocable.

The login endpoint rate-limits before it even looks the account up (so the limiter does not itself reveal which addresses exist), keyed on more than the address alone, and returns a generic 'Invalid credentials' for both unknown-email and bad-password. Registration is the exception — see SEC-04.

cleared.area: Privilege escalation via registration / mass assignment
cleared.detail: Self-registration hardcodes role = 'USER'; the role cannot be set from the request body. Entity writes flow through DTOs that only accept declared fields, and created_by / updated_by are set from the authenticated token after the body is spread, so authorship cannot be forged.
Confirmation and password-reset links are built from a server-configured base_url, not from the request Host header, so there is no host-header injection into the links delivered to users.

php/storage (including the new error logs, which record IP addresses) is gitignored. The database password is never returned in a response. The error handler runs with displayErrorDetails = false and returns generic messages to clients while writing detail to the server-side log — no stack traces or DSNs reach the client.

Every per-installation value - the database, the site secret, the IAM issuer and client id, the site's address and CORS origins - comes only from backend/config/*.local.php: gitignored, left out of the build, with no committed default, template fallback or environment variable. Without them index.php answers every request 503 not_set_up before any other code runs. setup.php writes them. On the hosting it demands a token only FTP access can read (a 192-bit value compared with hash_equals), writes a lock before anything else can fail, and deletes itself; it refuses http and localhost addresses there, so a development value cannot be left in. On a developer's machine it runs without a token only when three things hold at once - PHP's built-in server, a loopback REMOTE_ADDR, and a localhost Host header (which a DNS-rebinding page cannot send) - and even then every post must carry a nonce matching an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie. Its "Test connection" actions, which make the server connect to an address the form names, are gated exactly like the form, follow no redirects and fetch the IAM's key set and sign-in endpoint only on the issuer's own origin, so they are not an open SSRF. Secrets are never displayed back; config files are written 0600. Exercised on 2026-09-29 against throwaway databases: the refused token, the forged post, the stale nonce, the lock and the self-delete all behaved.
